title: You Think Finding Your Way Is Muscle Habit, Yet Single Brain Cells Draw Honeycomb Maps
description:
Experimental Chronicle — O'Keefe (1971) & May-Britt and Edvard Moser (2005): Place Cells, Hexagonal Grid Cells & Your Brain's Inner GPS, grounded in J. O'Keefe, J. Dostrovsky (1971) (Brain Research). Empirical findings show that in 1948 Edward Tolman claimed brains build internal 'Cognitive Maps', while behaviorists scoffed that 'maps in the head' were unscientific fairy tales. In *1971 (Brain Research), John O'Keefe and student Jonathan Dostrovsky at University College London listened to single CA1 hippocampal neurons* in freely exploring animals — instead of strapping heads still.

At the circuit level, this episode examines how temporal lobe, hippocampus, prefrontal cortex coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that O'Keefe discovered 8 neurons unlike anything ever recorded: Cell 1 ignored food, water, grooming, and sound anywhere else, firing exclusively whenever the animal walked through the NORTH-WEST corner; Cell 2 fired strictly by the SOUTH edge; Cell 3 strictly at CENTER — 'Place Cells' whose ensemble literally spelled out 'Where am I right now?'.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- J. O'Keefe, J. Dostrovsky (1971). The hippocampus as a spatial map. Preliminary evidence from unit activity in the freely-moving rat. Brain Research. https://doi.org/10.1016/0006-8993(71)90358-1
- Edvard, May-Britt Moser (2012). Edvard and May-Britt Moser. Current Biology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2012.06.076
- Alexandra O. Constantinescu, Jill X. O'Reilly, Timothy E. J. Behrens (2016). Organizing conceptual knowledge in humans with a gridlike code. Science. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aaf0941
